title: Positive monoid lengths and finite convolution
statement:
Let $G\cong\mathbf Z^r$ be a free abelian group of finite rank, meaning a free $\mathbf Z$-module with a finite basis [def-weil-pbc-free-module] and $P\subseteq G$ an additive submonoid generated by nonzero elements $g_1,\ldots,g_s$ (allow $s=0$). Let $w:G	o\mathbf Z$ be a group homomorphism strictly positive on $P\setminus\{0\}$. Every sum of $l$ nonzero elements of $P$ has positive weight when $l>0$, and a decomposition of $p$ into $l$ such elements has $l\le w(p)$. For every $p\in P$ the set of such lengths, allowing the empty sum for $p=0$, has an attained maximum $
u(p)\in\mathbf N$, and $
u(0)=0$. For every integer $M\ge0$, the set $\{p\in P:w(p)\le M\}$ is finite; for every integer $n\ge1$, $S_n=\{p\in P:
u(p)<n\}$ is finite. For every $p\in P$, the sets of pairs $(u,v)\in P^2$ and triples $(u,v,t)\in P^3$ with sum $p$ are finite. For any commutative ring $A$, the formulas $(a+c)_p=a_p+c_p$ and $(ac)_p=\sum_{u+v=p}a_uc_v$ equip $B=A^P$ with a commutative ring structure, with zero the zero family and unit $z^0$, where $z^p_q=1$ if $q=p$ and $0$ otherwise. The map $C:A	o B$, $C(a)=az^0$, is a unital ring homomorphism, $z^uz^v=z^{u+v}$, and $C(a)z^p$ is the family with sole possibly nonzero coefficient $a$ at $p$. For every $s_0\in P$ and $c\in B$, $(z^{s_0}c)_p=c_q$ when $p=s_0+q$ for $q\in P$, and is zero otherwise; such $q$ is unique. No completeness assumption on $A$ is made.

Not asserted to be a theorem stated in ILO.

proof.text: For $x\in P$, $w(x)\ge0$: it is zero if $x=0$ and is a positive integer otherwise. Thus, if $p=x_1+\cdots+x_l$ with every $x_j\ne0$, then $w(p)=\sum_jw(x_j)\ge l$; if $l>0$ this weight is positive. In particular no nonempty such sum is zero.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 1.

proof.text: For each p, the natural decomposition lengths are nonempty (the empty word for zero, the singleton otherwise) and bounded above by max(w(p),0) using step 1. Mathlib BddAbove.exists_isGreatest_of_nonempty gives an attained greatest length; choose this unique natural number as ν(p). Applying the bound to its attaining decomposition at zero proves ν(0)=0.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 2.

proof.text: By induction on membership in closure(range g), every p in P is the sum of a finite word of generator indices in Fin s: generators give singleton words, zero the empty word, and addition concatenates words. Every generator is nonzero. Converting a word to its finite sequence, step 1 bounds its length by w(p), hence by M.toNat when w(p)≤M and M≥0. Mathlib List.finite_length_le says the words over Fin s of length at most M.toNat form a finite set; their image under summation contains the weight sublevel set. This also covers s=0, where only the empty word exists.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 3.

proof.text: A generator word for p gives a decomposition into its word length many nonzero elements. The greatest-length property therefore bounds the word length by ν(p). If ν(p)<n the word has length less than n. Mathlib List.finite_length_lt says these words over Fin s form a finite set, whose summation image contains the length sublevel set. This includes s=0 and n=1 and does not reverse the inequality ν(p)≤w(p).

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 4.

proof.text: Fix $p\in P$ and put $K_p=\{x\in P:w(x)\le w(p)\}$. This is finite by step 3 because $w(p)\ge0$. If $u+v=p$, nonnegativity of both weights gives $u,v\in K_p$; if $u+v+t=p$, all three terms similarly belong to $K_p$. Thus the pair and triple sets are subsets of the finite sets $K_p^2$ and $K_p^3$.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 5.

proof.text: Define addition, zero and negatives coefficientwise on $B=A^P$, and define multiplication by the stated sum over the finite pair set from step 5. The additive abelian-group laws hold coefficient by coefficient in $A$. For each $p$, expanding $\sum_{u+v=p}(a_u+c_u)b_v$ by distributivity in $A$ gives $((a+c)b)_p=(ab)_p+(cb)_p$; expansion in the second factor gives the other distributive law. These finite-sum expansions follow by adjoining one summand at a time, starting with the empty sum; multiplying by the zero family gives zero.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 6.

proof.text: The swap $(u,v)\mapsto(v,u)$ is a bijection of the pair set over $p$, and $a_uc_v=c_va_u$ in $A$, so $(ac)_p=(ca)_p$. In $(z^0a)_p$ all terms with $u\ne0$ vanish, and the unique remaining pair is $(0,p)$, giving $a_p$. Thus $z^0$ is a left identity and, by commutativity, a right identity.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 7.

proof.text: For a fixed exponent p let D(p) be the subtype of pairs with sum p, finite by step 5. Expanding the two convolution bracketings and distributing multiplication over finite sums yields sums indexed respectively by Σ (h,t) in D(p), D(h) and Σ (u,k) in D(p), D(k). The bijection sends ((h,t),(u,v)) to ((u,v+t),(v,t)); its inverse sends ((u,k),(v,t)) to ((u+v,t),(u,v)). The defining sum equations and additive associativity verify membership and inverse identities. Fintype.sum_sigma and Fintype.sum_equiv identify the two sums using multiplicative associativity in A. These identities and steps 6--7 construct an actual CommRing on P→A; the natural and integer casts are the corresponding constants supported at zero.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 8.

proof.text: For $u,v\in P$, the coefficient $(z^uz^v)_p$ has a possibly nonzero summand only at the pair $(u,v)$; it is $1$ exactly if $p=u+v$. Consequently $z^uz^v=z^{u+v}$. Defining $C(a)$ to have coefficient $a$ at $0$ and zero elsewhere gives $C(a+b)=C(a)+C(b)$, $C(ab)=C(a)C(b)$, and $C(1)=z^0$ directly from the same pair calculation. Hence $C$ is a unital ring homomorphism, and $(C(a)z^p)_q$ is $a$ for $q=p$ and zero otherwise, as claimed.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 9.

proof.text: Finally, in $(z^{s_0}c)_p$ all summands with first coordinate different from $s_0$ vanish. If $p=s_0+q$ for $q\in P$, its sole remaining term is $c_q$; if there is no such $q$, the coefficient is zero. If $s_0+q=s_0+q'$, cancellation in the ambient group $G$ gives $q=q'$. Every sum above was finite, so none of these constructions or identities uses a topology or completeness on $A$.

source.place: Exposé VI §1.6(i)--(ii), printed p. 70 (PDF p. 76), formal monoid models; elementary coefficient argument supplied by Q53, not a theorem asserted in ILO. Step 10.
